Title: The Collapse
Text:
In the 22nd century, Earth was destroyed. It's not clear what happened, although the prevailing belief is that a scientific experiment spun wildly out of control. Whatever the cause, the planet was ripped apart, and electro-magnetic storms destroyed most of the other assets humanity had in the solar system.

Despite its colonization efforts, human civilization was still utterly dependent on Earth and Sol as its logistical, political, and resource centre.  The colonies were plunged into darkness and anarchy. The strong survived by taking from the weak, and a great many died. It was several generations before the situation stabilized, and by then there was little trace of the sophisticated technocratic culture that had taken humanity to the stars.

Title: Colony
Text:
Before the <link="collapse">Collapse</link>, humanity was on the verge of rapid colonization of the galaxy. Mining, research, and industrial installations had been built across scores of star systems, as states and corporations raced to exploit the possibilities of this new frontier. After the Collapse, these installations have become the only remaining living spaces for humanity, as the practical knowledge and economics that would be needed to build more have been lost.

A colony consists of several <link="installation">installations</link> in a system that are under the banner of a single ruling <link="house>house</link>. The practicalities of defense against outside aggressors creates pressure to unite under a single banner, and the lower travel time within a system lets the strongest house easily exert its power over the others.

When the power structure of a colony has been stable for a long time, it becomes widely accepted that its <link="head">ruler</link>'s bloodline is the <link="claims">legitimate authority</link> of the colony. Challengers will be judged more harshly, and should the house fall from power it will be expected to aggressively reclaim its position.

The typical population of a colony is between 100,000  to 250,000 people.

Colonies are part of <link="faction">factions</link>.

Title: House
Text: The basic unit of social organization is the House. Houses descend from the gangs that initially formed after the Collapse to control space and resources on the colonies. Some colonies have scores of houses that have carved up the colony between them. A house will control the lives of hundreds or thousands of commoners, but the most important people in it are its members; the head of the house, their family, and their trusted advisors. Members of a house always live in the same colony, though they may sometimes travel. When a couple marries, one of the partners will leave their house and join the house of their spouse. Note that your family members are not necessarily also members of your house. A House can be one of the following; - A noble house is the lowest form of house, and controls a section of a colony. - A ruling house is the noble house that rules the colony. It is headed by a baron. - A leading house is the ruling house on the capital of a faction. It is headed by a duke. - A great house is the leading house of the master faction of a league. It is headed by an archon. See Vassalage for a visual representation of these relationships. Information about your house is shown when you click on your house flag, or within the borders of the faction it rules on the map.

Title: Head of a House
Text: The head of a house is the individual who owns that house, and who controls it with an iron fist. They have the power of life and death over the house's members and indentured commoners, although customs and tradition restrains their hand. The head of a house that; - controls part of a colony is a Noble - rules a colony is a Baron - rules a faction is a Duke - rules a league is an Archon Barons, dukes, and archons are collectively referred to as rulers. See Vassalage for a visual representation of the political hierarchy. When the head of a house dies, the ownership of the house is inherited. If the legal head is underage, or in some other way unavailable to manage the house, an acting head is temporarily placed in charge. They are typically the spouse or a close relative of the legal head.

Title: Faction
Text:
<link="colony>Colonies</link> band together, either for protection, or because the ruling <link="house>house</link> of a colony is powerful enough to coerce nearby colonies to be <link="vassalage">vassals</link>.

A faction is ruled by a <link="head">duke</link>. A duke is obliged to protect their vassal <link="head">barons</link> and to address their <link="morality">grievances</link>. In return barons pay a <link="tax">tax</link> and must provide their colony's <link="fleet">fleet</link> when called to arms. Beyond those obligations, barons expect significant autonomy, and will engage in their own military adventures.

When the power structure of a faction has been stable for a long time, it becomes widely accepted that its duke's bloodline is the <link="claims">legitimate authority</link> of the faction, and that the faction should own its vassal colonies.

A single colony that is independent is also called a faction. Factions can be part of a <link="league">league</link>.

Title: League
Text: A league is a group of factions that is ruled by an archon. The league is the largest kind of political grouping. See Vassalage for a visual representation of the political hierarchy. The factions in a league are ruled by the vassal dukes of the archon. One of the factions in the league is the master faction. This faction is ruled personally by the archon. The archon also personally rules the capital system of this faction. An independent duke can become an archon by forming a vassal faction, however this is only a beneficial move if the duke is reaching their vassal limit. An independent duke can also become an archon if another duke agrees to become their vassal. A baron or vassal duke cannot have their own vassal dukes, and so cannot become an archon directly. However they could rebel against their political hierarchy, making them an independent duke. When a faction has been the vassal of a league for a long time, the master faction gains a claim to be the master of the vassal.

Title: Inheritance
Text:
The warlords that initially seized power after <link="collapse">the Collapse</link> chose family members as their successors. Over time, bloodline inheritance has become the social and political norm, forming the basis for legitimate authority to rule.

When an individual dies, their firstborn child (depending on the applicable <link="succession">succession</link> rule) inherits their possessions and their <link="claims">authority</link>. They also inherit their <link="morality">grievances</link> and accountabililty for their <link="morality">crimes</link>. If a child inherits a position of power that they are still too young to hold, an acting <link="head">head</link> is temporarily appointed until they become of age. You can see the line of succession for any <link="house">house</link> or <link="colony">colony</link> by focusing on it.

If a deceased <link="head">baron</link> has no natural heir, it falls upon the <link="head">duke</link> of their <link="faction">faction</link> to appoint a new one. If a deceased duke or archon has no natural heir, their most senior vassal takes over their <link="domain">domain</link>.

If a duke or archon inherits a faction, the two factions are merged under the banner of the higher ranking one. If a baron inherits a faction, their <link="colony">colony</link> becomes the capital system of that faction. If a baron inherits a faction, or a <link="vassalage">vassal</link> duke inherits a master faction, they cease to be vassals of their former master without conflict or dishonor.

A <link="league">league</link> is inherited if its master faction is inherited.

If a duke or archon inherits a colony, that colony becomes part of their faction. If a baron inherits a colony, they must choose a character who will become its new baron, since they cannot personally rule both colonies.

When a noble inherits a colony or faction, their house takes over that territory and is merged with the previous house that ruled it. When a ruler inherits a noble house, that house is merged into their own.

Title: House Size Limit
Text:
Humanity lacks the knowledge to build new <link="colony">colonies</link> or significantly expand existing ones, so there is a limit on how many people can be supported. This has created enormous social pressure to limit population growth and the excessive consumption of colony resources.

As the <link="head">head</link> of a <link="house">house</link>, you must limit its members. The maximum size that is considered fair depends on your gross <link="houseincome">income</link>. The limit is visible when you focus on your house (shown as "Members: X/Y"). Hovering over it will show the relationship to your income.

You limit the size of your house by managing the number of <link="marriage">marriages</link> and children that the house members have. Each couple can have a single child, but need your permission to have more.

Title: Domain
Text:
The domain of a <link="house">house</link> is the region it controls, i.e. the domain of;
- a ruling house is the <link="colony">colony</link>
- a leading house is the <link="faction">faction</link>
- a great house is the <link="league">league</link>

See <link="vassalage">Vassalage</link> for a visual representation of the political hierarchy.

For easier navigation, when you click on a leading or great house's flag, you are shown information about that house's domain (i.e. it's faction or league) as well as information about the house.

Title: Vassalage
Text: The relationship between rulers in the galaxy is that of vassalage; a system of mutual obligation between the master and subject. The master provides protection and justice, while the subject provides military and economic support. In a faction, a duke has barons as vassals. Each baron pays a tax to the duke, and must bring their military fleet when called upon. The baron in turn has their own vassals; the nobles that control the colony. Thus when a duke goes to war, their fleet is composed of the ships of all the houses on all the colonies of their faction. A duke may by independent, but they may also be a vassal of an archon. Archons rule leagues of factions, and sit at the top of the political hierarchy. Vassals enjoy considerable autonomy, largely because of the distances between colonies. As a result, even powerful houses have limited tools to directly control their subjects, and holding together a large faction or league can be more challenging than conquering it. When a ruler willingly submits to becoming the vassal of another, any grievances between them are forgotten. Note that not all the rulers within another ruler's territory are their direct vassals. The vassal barons of a duke who is the vassal of an archon are indirect vassals of the archon. Unless specified, "vassal" means "direct vassal".

Title: Taxation
Text:
Tax is the primary source of <link="houseincome">income</link> for <link="head">dukes</link> and <link="head">archons</link>. Each direct <link="vassalage">vassal</link> of a house pays tribute to their master house.

There are three levels of tax that you can set on your ruler vassals; Low (<v>10%</v>), Medium (<v>20%</v>), or High (<v>30%</v>). At Low and High levels of tax your vassals will experience an <link="opinion">opinion</link> bonus or penalty respectively.

You can increase the amount of tax you get from a specific vassal, without negatively impacting their opinion of you, by using the <link="administration">Assist Tax Collection</link> <link="assignments">assignment</link>.

Title: Military Fleets
Text:
Each <link="house">house</link> derives its power from the military force it can bring to bear to protect its <link="domain">territory</link> or threaten its rivals.

Each house maintains some form of private fleet. A <link="vassalage">vassal</link> house is obliged to participate in the military adventures of its master. Thus, while a <link="head">baron</link> might have a small personal fleet, they can command a fleet of the combined military vessels of their <link="colony">colony</link> when they need to defend it or answer a call to arms of their master. Similarly, a <link="head">duke</link> can command the combined fleets of their <link="faction">faction</link>, and an <link="head">archon</link> can command the combined fleets of their <link="league">league</link>.

In practice, when you attack or defend a particular location, you will only be calling upon the vassals that are close to that location, as only they will be able to supply a significant portion of their fleet. If you click or hover over a star system on the map you will be shown the size of the combined fleet you can bring to bear at that location if all vassals in range answered your call.

To your benefit, houses in a colony are motivated to build and maintain the largest private fleet they can to defend themselves. A colony's fleet is built with diminishing returns, i.e. as the fleet grows larger, it grows more slowly. There is a maximum fleet size a colony can support that is directly tied to the amount of <h>Wealth</h> generated by its <link="installation">installations</link>. A colony has a natural fleet <link="fleetcomposition">composition</link> based on the surviving production facilities available to it.

As a ruler you manage the combined fleet of your <link="domain">domain</link> indirectly;
- You can accelerate fleet building in a specific colony using the <link="administration">Rebuild Fleet</link> <link="assignments">assignment</link>.
- You can increase the maximum size of a colony's fleet by repairing installations that generate <h>Wealth</h>.
- You can gradually shift the composition of the fleet that the houses on a specific colony build and maintain using the <link="technology">Shift Fleet Composition</link> assignment.

Title: Vassal Limit
Text:
There is a limit to how many <link="vassalage">vassals</link> you can have without penalty. This is shown for your <link="house">house</link> in the bottom toolbar, to the right of your character's portrait. The limit is calculated as the sum of the following factors:
- Base Value of <v>3</v>
- Your house's score in <link="administration">Administration</link> (<pv>+1</pv> for each <v>50</v> points)
- Your house's score in <link="technology">Technology</link> (<pv>+1</pv> for each <v>75</v> points)
- Your house's <link="houseincome">gross income</link> (<pv>+1</pv> for each <v>20</v><#dcab00><sprite name="icon_money" tint=1></color>)
- Using the <link="technology">Monitor Vassals</link> <link="assignments">assignment</link> (<pv>+1</pv> to <pv>+3</pv> based on effectiveness)
- Bonuses provided by some <link="installation">installations</link>, if they are within range of your home system

When your house has too many vassals you suffer two penalties;
- Your gross income is reduced by a fraction equal to the number of excess vassals divided by the vassal limit, e.g. if you have <v>7</v> vassals against a limit of <v>5</v>, your gross income is reduced by (<v>7</v>-<v>5</v>)/<v>5</v> = <v>2</v>/<v>5</v>.
- Your <link="ap">AP</link> is reduced by the number of excess vassals

If you are an <link="head">archon</link>, you can reduce your direct vassals by transferring control of barons to your vassal dukes. If you are an independent duke, you can <link="formvassal">form a vassal faction</link> within your territory, and transfer control of barons to your new vassal duke. If you are a vassal duke you cannot reduce your direct vassals without reducing the size of your territory. In extremis, you can grant a vassal independence from you.

Title: Action Points (AP)
Text: Each character gets 12 Action Points (AP) per turn, which represents the amount of time they have to focus on different activities. Actions usually cost some AP to trigger, and you can no longer effectively act when you run out of AP. There are standard modifiers to AP per turn: - -4 to +4 based on your happiness at the end of the last turn. - If you have too many vassals, you get -1 AP for each vassal over the limit. At the end of the turn, any AP you have not used is converted into income for your house. Each unused AP point is converted to 0.5<#dcab00>. Important Note: Do not feel that you must spend all your AP. AP acts as a limit to how much you can do in a single turn, but there will be some turns (especially when your empire is small), where there isn't much you can meaningfully do to improve your position. Lie in wait, and pounce when an opportunity arises.

Title: Happiness
Text:
The game tracks the overall mood of each character, which changes based on the following factors;
- The events that happen to that character directly
- The ongoing circumstances that are part of that character's life
- The ongoing circumstances or events that happen to other characters they care about

Different characters will react more or less strongly to the same event based on their <link="traits">traits</link>. For example, a cowardly <link="head">ruler</link> will react more negatively to being attacked.

You can examine the reasons why a particular character is happy by focusing on that character. Note that the overall value (on a scale of <nv>-100</nv> to <pv>100</pv>) is not a simple sum of the contribution of each reason. As a character becomes significantly happy or unhappy, each source of happiness has progressively less effect (i.e. it has diminishing returns).

When you are happy;
- You are better liked by others
- You improve your <link="skill">skills</link> more quickly
- You get a bonus to your <link="ap">AP</link>
- You get a bonus to your <link="house">house</link>'s <link="houseareas">capability scores</link>

Conversely, when you are unhappy you will receive a penalty in these areas.

Title: House Areas
Text:
The activities that a <link="house">house</link> carries out are broken down into five areas;
- <link="administration">Administration</link>
- <link="military">Military</link>
- <link="diplomacy">Diplomacy</link>
- <link="security">Security</link>
- <link="technology">Technology</link>

For each area, a member is appointed as the <link="councilmember">council member</link> responsible for that area.

For your house, the House Members UI tab shows you the assigned council member and your house's score in each area. An area score determines the strength of a set of passive effects. It is based on;
- Your <link="skill">skills</link>
- The skills of the relevant <link="councilmember">council member</link>
- Your <link="happiness">happiness</link>
- The council member's happiness
- The council member's <link="opinion">opinion</link> of you

Mouse over the value to see more details.

Title: Justice
Text: The formal legal system in the colonies died in the Collapse, but social and political behaviour is still constrained by a set of widely accepted norms that have evolved to limit aggression and abuse of power. When you contravene these norms you commit a crime and lose honor. On the other hand, if you go above and beyond what is expected of you to help your fellow man, you gain honor. The victim of a crime gets a grievance against their wrongdoer. If they then act in a way that would normally be considered dishonorable towards the wrongdoer, they are instead seen as seeking justified revenge, and will not lose honor so long as their revenge is proportional. For example, executing someone is normally dishonorable behaviour, but you will be justified in executing a noble that rebelled against you. Grievances are forgotten over time; how long depends on the seriousness of the crime. While they persist, they are inherited. The acting head of a house can seek revenge for crimes committed against the legal head of the house. Parents can seek revenge for crimes committed against their underage children, if those children are members of the same house. Committing a crime against someone who owes you a favour will let them off the hook for that favour. You can try to frame someone for dishonorable behaviour using the Defame assignment. Charging If an individual wrongs someone who cannot directly seek revenge themselves, and the crimes are sufficiently serious, the victim may be able to demand justice from a ruler. The ruler to whom the charge is made depends on the social and political relationships between the victim and the criminal, and the nature of the crime. They may be; - The master of the victim - The master of the criminal - A kin member of the victim who is a ruler If a character would come to you to demand justice for a particular grievance, you can pre-emptively approach them and offer to avenge it. This is useful if you want to move against a character under the pretense of righteousness. If you are charged, you are then able to punish the criminal or to charge another ruler in turn who may be better placed to punish. Depending on the severity of the crimes and the relationship to the victim; you may be honor-bound to seek revenge within 2 turns, unless a war prevents them from doing so. This information is shown in the Justice Panel when focusing on yourself. Avenging a particularly serious crime will improve your reputation. If the relevant social and political relationships change, and the ruler to whom the charge should be made changes, the original charge is invalidated, and that ruler may no longer avenge the crimes. If a ruler is charged but fails to avenge the crime, they may not be charged again until several years pass.

Title: Administration
Text: The administrative function of a ruling house manages logistics within its domain, oversees its colony, and collects tax. Passive Effects - Increases your income - Increases the number of vassals you can have The strength of these effects is proportional to the score of the house in Administration. Assignments - Assist Tax Collection: Increases the amount of tax collected from a vassal ruler. - Repair Installation: Repairs an installation in a colony so as to generate it's benefits. - Rebuild Colony: Repairs a derelict colony, repopulates it, and makes it part of your faction. - Rebuild Fleet: Increases the rate at which a colony's fleet will reach its maximum size.

Title: Military
Text: The root of a house's power is its capability to exert military force when necessary. The military team of a house is responsible for preparing the house's fleet, training the rank and file, and for coordinating and leading vassal fleets when called to war. Passive Effects - Provides a strength bonus to your combined fleet in combats that your house leads - Provides a strength bonus to your home system's fleet in combat, whether you are the fleet leader or a participant The strength of these effects is proportional to the score of the house in Military. Assignments - Improve Defense: Gives your fleet a defense bonus in a particular location. - Improve Attack: Gives your fleet an attack bonus in a particular location. Takes time to ramp up. - Hide Fleet Movements: Improve your chances of maintaining surprise when a particular vassal joins your fleet. - Quell Unrest: Reduce the likelihood of a system rebellion on your colony.

Title: Diplomacy
Text: The backbone of your power is your military might. But above that foundation, power lies in the game of politics between houses. Your diplomacy team is responsible for presenting your house's activities in the best possible light, disseminating propaganda about you and your actions that increase your popularity. Passive Effects - Gives a bonus opinion modifier to every character's opinion of you, particularly your vassal rulers. - Gives a bonus opinion modifier to every character's opinion of members of your house. The strength of these effects is proportional to the score of the house in Diplomacy. Assignments - Improve Relations: Gradually increase a character's opinion of you. - Defame: Frame a character for dishonorable behaviour they did not commit. - Spread Dissent: Fan the flames of rebellion on a colony. - Acquire Claim: Convince the public that your faction has an owning claim on a particular colony.

Title: Security
Text: The security team of a house is responsible for keeping its members safe, and for discovering information that the house can use to its advantage. Passive Effects - Provides a chance of discovering secrets involving your capital system and the characters in it, including visitors. - Reduces the effectiveness of foreign Assassinate, Defame, Spread Dissent, and Spy Network assignments against your house. The strength of these effects is proportional to the score of the house in Security. Assignments - Assassinate: Secretly kill a character. - Protect: Make a character harder to Assassinate. - Cover Up Secret: Gradually make a secret harder to discover. - Spy Network: Discover secrets, reduce enemy attack surprise, and counter enemy spy networks.

Title: Technology
Text: The technology team of a house are responsible for maintaining our knowledge of how to use the machines and devices that remain from before The Collapse, and to investigate and acquire any more that we may come across in ruined colonies and other forgotten installations. Passive Effects - Determines the rate at which Expedition Events will trigger - Reduces the chance of illness, and increases the chance of recovery from illness - Reduces the chance of bad outcomes during childbirth - Increases the rate of skill buildup by members of the house - Increases the maximum number of vassals the house can have The strength of these effects is proportional to the score of the house in Technology. Assignments - Provide Medical Attention: Improve health outcomes for a character. Increase probability of having a child. - Train: Increases a character's skill. - Shift Fleet Composition: Gradually change the composition of the fleet that is maintained by a particular colony. - Monitor Vassals: Increase the number of direct vassals you can manage.

Title: Health
Text: Medical care in the colonies is poor. Knowledge of biology and anatomy within the population is non-existent. Pathogens have evolved for which we have no synthesizeable drugs. Overcrowding, poor hygiene, poor diet, and the abnormal living conditions contribute to high rates of disease and ill health, at least within the general population. Ill characters can continue to perform most tasks, but they get a -50% modifier to their skills. An ill character who gets better may remain sickly. Sickly characters get ill and have negative health outcomes more frequently. The probability that a member of your house falls ill, or gets better when they are ill, generally depends on your house's technology score. You can also use the Medical Care assignment to safeguard the health of specific members of your house.

Title: Opinion and Reputation
Text: The game tracks the opinion every character has of each other character that they are aware of. This opinion is based primarily on whether; - the character likes the personality of the other character - the other character has behaved honorably - the other character has earned respect, i.e. whether that have demonstrated strength or weakness - the other character has done things that have helped or hurt them - the other character has done things that have helped or hurt their friends or enemies Characters will form stronger or weaker opinions of the same event based on their traits. For example, honorable characters will disapprove more strongly of dishonorable behaviour. Opinions that are based on events will fade over time. Underneath character portraits there is a bar that shows the opinion that character has of the character which you are hovering over. If you are not hovering over another character, the opinion shown will be of the character in the first quickbar slot. This is the contrasted character. If there is no contrasted character, and you are not hovering over another character, the character's opinion of you will be shown. To see the detailed reason behind the opinion, focus on the character whose opinions you want to see, and the first tab (Feelings) will contain a full list of the opinions that character has of the other character. A character's opinion of another character is partly personal, i.e. formed by actions that effected them or their peers. But it also includes a set of common opinions that are widely held about that character. These opinions are that character's reputation, and correspond to the first three items in the list above. You can see a character's reputation by clicking on them. You can improve a character's opinion of you by acting more favourably towards them and their loved ones, or by increasing your reputation. If they are not a member of your house you can also use the Improve Relations assignment.

Title: Council Member
Text:
The <link="head">head</link> of a <link="house">house</link> has a council, on which sit the house members that are responsible for the five <link="houseareas">house areas</link>. A house's score in each area is primarily based on the council member assigned to that area, so you will usually want your ablest member for each area on the council.

Placing someone to the council is a permanent privilege, and it is <link="morality">dishonorable</link> to replace them. In addition, you are honor-bound to assign one of the council positions to your <link="marriage">spouse</link>.

Title: Skills
Text:
Every character has a skill level in five different skills, each of which corresponds to a house <link="houseareas">area</link>:
- <link="administration">Administration</link>
- <link="military">Military</link>
- <link="diplomacy">Diplomacy</link>
- <link="security">Security</link>
- <link="technology">Technology</link>

The skill of a character determines their effectiveness in carrying out <link="assignments">assignments</link>, and the amount they will contribute to the house score in an area if they are appointed to the <link="councilmember">council</link>.

Children gradually improve in the skills they are interested in until they come of age. Children who have been assigned a <link="guardianship">guardian</link> will improve more quickly in the primary skills of that guardian. After they become an adult, a character's skills can be improved in the following ways:
- Carrying out an <link="assignments">assignment</link>
- Using the <link="technology">Train</link> assignment
- The <link="head">head</link> of a house slowly improves their skills in all areas

Title: Marriage
Text:
Marriage is one of the most important institutions in post-<link="collapse">Collapse</link> culture, for two reasons;
- Acting in bad faith towards one's kin is <link="opinion">dishonorable</link>. Marrying into a family is a good way to discourage them from seeing you as a military target. In general, a <link="morality">crime</link> against a family member is considered a more heinous crime. Kin members are also obliged to defend each other from <link="combat">aggression</link>.
- As legitimate power can only be transferred through <link="inheritance">inheritance</link>, marriage is one of the key ways an ambitious <link="house">house</link> or individual can gain power.

Your marriage is an ongoing source of <link="happiness">happiness</link> or unhappiness for your character, depending on how much you like your spouse and whether they are away from your <link="colony">home system</link>.

Because of how valuable marriage is to form alliances amongst the nobility (and keep the peace), dissolving a marriage through divorce is normally dishonorable.

When two members from different houses are married, the lesser partner becomes a member of the more important partner's house. The more important partner is determined by the first relevant rule;
- the character who is higher in a <link="inheritance">line of succession</link> to become a <link="head">ruler</link>
- the character who stands to inherit a higher ranking house
- the older character

If two rulers get married, they will remain the heads of their respective house and live seperately.

The spouse of a ruler has rights by virtue of their position. If an acting <link="head">head</link> must take the reins temporarily, they are usually chosen. The ruler is also honor-bound to place them on their <link="councilmember">council</link>.

Characters are not free to arrange their own marriages. Instead, for each character there is a <link="marriageauthority">marriage authority</link> who can marry them off or divorce their marriage.

Title: Codex
Text:
Welcome to the Star Dynasties Codex!

This is a library of information about the setting and game rules of Star Dynasties.  Use the list on the left to navigate to the topic of your choice, or click on highlighted topics in the text. 

These topics will help you understanding the setting:

- <link="colony">Colonies</link>

These topics will help you understand the core mechanics of the game:
