Title: Claims
Text:
When the power structure in a region has been stable for a long time, it comes to be seen as the legitimate structure for that region. Aggression aimed at usurping or conquering it away from its masters is seen as more <link="morality">dishonorable</link>, since they have a rightful claim to that region.

A claim can be credible (weak) or legitimate (strong).

There are the following kinds of claims;
- A character can have a claim to rule a <link="colony">colony</link>
- A character can have a claim to rule a <link="faction">faction</link>
- A faction can have a claim to own a colony
- A faction can have a claim to have another faction as its <link="vassalage">vassal</link>

Character claims are <link="inheritance">inherited</link>.

An unexercised claim will fade over time. Characters that have a claim, but are not themselves in power, will pass on a weaker version of their claim to their children (or no claim at all). Factions that no longer possess the colonies or vassal factions they claim will lose those claims over time.

Faction claims to own colonies can be acquired using the <link="diplomacy">Acquire Claim</link> <link="assignments">assignment</link>.

Title: Claim Pressing
Text: You press a claim by helping a claimant (potentially yourself) gain their rightful authority. Pressing a claim justifies aggression that is normally a crime. If you help someone else press a claim, you are championing that claim. You are always justified in trying to press your own claims, even if you fail multiple times. However you cannot champion another's claim repeatedly until some time has passed. Claims can be pressed directly in the following ways; - A duke or archon can press a character's claim to be the ruler of one of the vassal colonies in their faction by deposing that colony's current ruler and replacing them - An archon can press a character's claim to be the ruler of one of their vassal factions by deposing that faction's current ruler and replacing them - A duke or archon can press a character's claim to rule a dead faction by resurrecting that faction within their territory, if some of it is claimed by the dead faction - A duke or archon can press a character's claim to rule a foreign faction or its capital by declaring war on it - A duke or archon can press a faction's claim to own one of their vassal colonies by transferring ownership of the colony to that faction - A duke or archon can press a faction's claim to own their capital system by surrendering ownership of their faction - A duke can press an independent faction's claim to be their faction's master by becoming that faction's vassal - A vassal duke can press an independent faction's claim to be their faction's master by betraying their current master and switching allegiance - An archon can press an independent faction's claim to be the master of one of their vassal factions by transferring ownership of the vassal faction to that faction - A ruler can press various claims within their master's territory by rebelling against them You can only champion a claim of a direct subject. If a ruler cannot press a claim directly they may still be able to champion it. If the claim relates to something outside their territory, they champion it by making a demand from the ruler whose territory it resides in. If the claim relates to something within their territory, they champion it by making a demand from the vassal that can press it or champion it in turn. When a ruler makes a demand to another ruler to press or champion a claim, the consequence of refusal is always war or rebellion.

Title: Combat
Text: When violence erupts between two houses, it is usually settled through a battle between the combined fleets that those houses can muster. Assigning a Commander Your first decision when engaged in a combat is to choose the commander that will lead the combat. Commanders have a skill level and different tactics that they bring to an engagement. You can not use a commander in multiple locations in the same turn unless those locations are nearby. If no one is available to command the fleet, you cannot fight. Buildup You and your opponent will then progressively build up your fleets for the engagement. In turn you will choose the ruler of a colony that is in range of the combat location and ask for their support. Different rulers will have different obligations to help you; - Vassals are honor-bound to answer a call to arms by their master - A master is honor-bound to defend a vassal when they are attacked by someone who is not also their vassal - A vassal is obliged not to support the side their master is fighting against, and vice versa - If a duke or archon provides their support, their vassals become obliged to provide their support if asked - The kin of the defender usually have an obligation to help them Both sides may try to strike deals to bring in a neutral party on their side, and pay mercenaries to pad their fleets. The closer a ruler's colony is to the combat location, the more of their military they can provide. You can still ask for support from rulers that are outside the combat range if they have vassals that are within the range, as that ruler's support will oblige their vassals to aid you. To provide their military, a ruler must also have a path by which they can reach the combat location through your territory, or the territory of rulers that have agreed to support you. Each ruler that joins the combat appoints a commander that is responsible for their colony's sub-fleet. The attacker must pay AP for each action they take during buildup. Buildup ends when they choose to launch their attack, however the defender gets 4 additional actions at this point. The attacker can choose to retreat from the attack. The defender may attempt to negotiate this retreat. Surprise When an attacker starts a combat buildup, they usually start with the element of surprise. While they have surprise, they ask rulers to join their fleet without the defender acting in turn, thus reducing the number of buildup actions the defender will take. Surprise can be lost in two ways; - A ruler you ask for support betrays the attack to the defender. You can minimize the risk of this by not asking rulers that have some loyalty to the defender, until you lose surprise. - Fleet movements are detected by agents of the defender. The chance of this happening becomes progressively larger for each additional ruler that joins your fleet. You can minimize the risk of this by using the Hide Fleet Movemements assignment. Conversely, you can increase the chances you detect enemy fleet movements by using the Spy Network assignment. Resolution The combat itself happens over three rounds. In each round; - Both sides pick a combat tactic to use (in secret), from the tactics that have not yet been used in that combat (the Attack and Retreat tactics can always be used). - Both sides make a damage roll. This determines the base damage dealt that round as a % of fleet strength. - Both sides deal damage to the opponent's fleet, based on; the size of their fleet, their damage roll, the respective composition of the fleets, and the tactics in play. The commanders that have been assigned to the fleet can be injured or killed during combat. If this happens before the end of combat, the portion of the fleet that commander is responsible for is reduced in strength for the remainder of combat. The winning side is the one with the largest fleet at the end of the three rounds, or the remaining side if the other retreats. You can improve your chances of victory in a particular location using the Improve Defense and Improve Attack assignments. Post-Combat Recovery A small portion of the damage inflicted to the colony fleet of each ruler is repaired. The amount repaired depends on the Military skill of the commander that colony's ruler chose.

Title: Space Travel
Text:
Even before the <link="collapse">Collapse</link>, no satisfactory explanation had been found for the existence of "star lanes", lattices of perturbations in space through which ships equipped with specialized drives can travel at great speeds. Humanity's initial exploration of the galaxy followed those strands that had fortunately linked two star systems.

Despite the existence of star lanes, travel between <link="colony">colonies</link> is slow. A ruler's best courier might manage a hop in a day or two. For the disintegrating trading vessels that trickle goods, visitors, and less important communications between colonies, a hop will take weeks.

As a result, colonies in the same territory enjoy considerable autonomy.

Title: Fleet Assignment
Text: When a <link="house">house</link> mounts an attack or defense, a <link="fleet">fleet</link> commander must be chosen from the house members assigned to <link="military">Military</link>. A fleet operation can take several weeks or months, given the time taken to <link="spacetravel">travel</link> between systems, so a commander sent to manage a fleet at a <link="colony">colony</link> can only be assigned to fleet operations that take place in systems nearby to that colony for a turn.

Title: System Rebellion
Text:
Unrest can grow on a <link="colony">colony</link>. When it reaches a critical threshold, a noble <link="house">house</link> leads a rebellion against its <link="head">ruler</link>.  The Population Unrest panel tracks the causes of dissatisfaction on the colony and the progress of unrest on it.

Some standard reasons for discontent are;
- Small number of liveable <link="installation">installations</link> in the colony
- The <link="head">baron</link> has a poor <link="opinion">reputation</link>
- The <link="head">duke</link> of the colony's <link="faction">faction</link> has a poor reputation
- The <link="head">archon</link> of the colony's league has a poor reputation
- The ruler is not the <link="claims">legitimate</link> ruler of the colony
- The system is not legitimately a member of its owning faction

External houses can actively try to provoke rebellion in a colony using the <link="diplomacy">Spread Dissent</link> <link="assignments">assignment</link>. Conversely, the ruling house can use the <link="military">Quell Unrest</link> assignment to suppress dissent.

When a system rebellion starts, the colony's <link="fleet">fleet</link> is split between rebels and loyalists and a <link="combat">combat</link> starts. Both sides will typically ask for help from nearby colonies. Most rebellions are doomed to fail, since even unpopular ruling houses usually have stronger relationships with houses from other colonies than the rebelling noble house.

If the rebel house wins the combat, it takes over as the new ruling house of the colony. By default, the colony remains a legitimate member and <link="vassalage">vassal</link> of its faction. However, a successful rebellion on a faction's capital system will dissolve the faction.

If the ruling house wins the combat, the rebellion is unsuccessful. Any surviving military on both sides is consolidated back into the colony fleet.

Title: Economy and Wealth
Text: Most of the inhabitants of the colonies work and live directly within the territory their patron house controls. For labouring in the hydroponic farms, mines, and shipyards they are fed and housed in cramped quarters. Skilled workers may be rewarded with better conditions, but few ever see any money. Even noble houses conduct much of their trade in goods or services directly, bartering food for ore, or exploiting whatever technology that house was lucky enough to end up controlling within its territory. However the universal need for viridium, a rare metal that is vital for ship construction and maintenance, has led to its adoption as a common currency, facilitating longer distance trade. Houses with vassals take a close interest in their economic activities, trying to find ways to improve the productivity of their territory as a whole. Ruling houses also sometimes use their wealth to improve common areas of the colony, reasoning that the increase in tribute over time will make up for their short term generosity.

Title: House Income
Text:
As a <link="head">ruler</link>, you have two main sources of income;
- the wealth you extract from your <link="colony">colony</link>
- the <link="tax">taxes</link> you levy on your vassal rulers

You can see a breakdown of your income and expenses by focusing on your <link="house">house</link>.

You can improve your income by;
- repairing <link="installation">installations</link> in your colony that provide <h>Wealth</h>
- increasing your house's <link="houseareas">score</link> in <link="administration">Administration</link>
- raising the <link="tax">tax rate</link> on your <link="vassalage">vassal rulers</link>
- using the Assist Tax Collection <link="assignments">assignment</link>

Title: Derelict Colonies
Text:
<link="house">Houses</link> expend considerable energy simply maintaining the <link="colony">colony</link> installations in which they reside. Bases have been patched and re-patched for hundreds of years, and rapidly decay without constant attention.

If all of a colony's <link="installation">installations</link> fall into disrepair, the colony is abandoned and its houses flee into destitution to nearby colonies.

A ruler can use the <link="administration">Rebuild Colony</link> <link="assignments">assignment</link> to repair the main installation of a derelict colony and repopulate it.

Title: Feasts
Text:
When a <link="house">house</link> is blessed with good fortune, it is customary for that house to throw a feast, inviting its <link="vassalage">vassals</link> and peers from nearby <link="colony">colonies</link> . When a house does not celebrate its successes, its <link="head">head</link> loses <link="opinion">respect</link>. Conversely, a successful feast can increase one's prestige.

Apart from special occasions, <link="head">dukes</link> and <link="head">archons</link> can also host a feast in someone's honor. Hosting a feast brings <link="opinion">prestige</link> to the guest of honor as well, for which they are usually grateful.

The cost of a feast scales with the number of rulers invited. Depending on the occasion, some rulers will expect an invite and will be annoyed at being snubbed.

A ruler or leader invited to a feast takes along a small entourage. With so much nobility mixing together, there is always some intrigue as a result. The highlight of the feast is its <link="tournament">tournament</link>.

Title: Tournaments
Text:
A common element of a <link="feast">feast</link> is the tournament. 

Each <link="head">ruler</link> that is attending the feast will submit a champion from their party. The winner of the tournament and their master <link="opinion">gain prestige</link>. A ruler can participate directly in the tournament, but participants risk <link="health">injury</link>.

In each bout of the tournament, you can instruct your champion to fight normally, fight aggressively, or throw the fight. Fighting aggressively increases the chance of victory, but also the chance of injury. Throwing a fight minimizes injury, and may be a good choice if you do not wish to anger your opponent. Note that if both participants are trying to throw the fight, you may still end up as the winner.

Title: Quickbar
Text:
In the bottom left of the UI you have a set of bookmarks for characters, star systems (i.e. <link="colony">colonies</link>), and <link="domain">domains</link> (i.e. <link="house">houses</link>, <link="faction">factions</link>, and <link="league">leagues</link>).

You place something in the quickbar by dragging it to a slot, or by Ctrl+Right-clicking on it to place it in the first available slot. Similarly you can clear a slot by Ctrl+Right-clicking it, or by dragging its content out and releasing it.

The first slot of the quickbar is special and only takes characters. When a character is in this slot, it is the contrast character, and other character portraits will show that character's <link="opinion">opinion</link> of the contrast character. You can place a character in the first quickbar slot by Ctrl-clicking it.

Title: Secrets
Text:
Some actions and events are only visible to the characters that are involved in them. A subset of these hidden events create <h>secrets</h>, i.e. some kind of evidence that can be used to show what happened, but that the characters would prefer to keep hidden.

Each turn there is a small chance that other characters that know you will discover one of your secrets. Secrets have a <h>discovery difficulty</h> which is on a scale from "Easy" to "Very Hard".

You have access to a Cover Up Secret <link="assignments">assignment</link> by which the evidence for a secret will eventually be destroyed, and the discovery difficulty of a secret will become "Never". Some secrets will automatically get harder to discover as time passes and eventually expire - this is shown when you hover over the secret's discovery difficulty.

You can actively try to discover the secrets of other characters (if they have any) by using the Spy Network <link="assignments">assignment</link>.

If you become aware of another character's secret you can usually <h>reveal</h> it publically, potentially damaging their political standing. If the secret was about a <link="morality">crime</link> they committed, the victim will get a grievance against them when the secret is revealed. You could also use the secret as blackmail, by making a <link="negotiation">request</link> and threatening to reveal it. Once used as blackmail, a secret can no longer be revealed by you. A secret with discovery difficulty of "Never" cannot be discovered, but it is usually still possible to reveal it or blackmail a character with it.

Title: War
Text:
When relationships between two leading <link="house">houses</link> break down, one side can declare war on the other if their territories are <link="map">nearby</link>, or threaten war if some demand is not met. Declaring war is normally <link="morality">dishonorable</link>. A war becomes justified if it is declared to avenge a crime, or to champion a <link="claims">claim</link> within the defender's <link="domain">domain</link>.

If a war is justified on the basis of a claim, the attacking <link="head">ruler</link> will still lose standing if they do not honor the claim at the first opportunity. For example, if the war was started to champion a character's claim to rule a <link="colony">colony</link>, then the ruler is honor-bound to install that character as the colony's ruler when it is conquered. If a war is on the basis of a claim, the defender can end the war at any time by accepting to <link="championing">press the claim</link>.

When an <link="head">archon</link> is at war, all the <link="faction">factions</link> in their <link="league">league</link> are considered at war with the enemy. Some political actions are not possible between houses whose respective <link="domain">domains</link> are at war. Similarly, a faction at war is constrained from trading away territory that is <link="map">nearby</link> to the enemy.

When war is declared, the attacking house will automatically recall its members before the war is declared. However any other character from either side that is carrying out an <link="assignments">assignment</link> in the territory of the enemy will be justifiably <link="arrest">arrested</link>.

While at war, any duke or archon on either side can attack and <link="attack">conquer</link> systems in the opponent's territory. When a system is attacked in war, the defense is always the responsibility of the ruler of its faction, even if it is part of a league. If a system is conquered, the victor may choose to replace its baron with a more trusted <link="vassalage">vassal</link>. Annexing systems that one has no claim to is dishonorable.

The war ends when the capital system of one side is conquered, or when both sides agree to peace. A war is also considered to have died out if neither side carries out any aggressive action or makes a demand for ten turns. However a war does not automatically end if the claim the attacker was championing is no longer relevant.

A finished war that was profitable is cause for <link="feast">celebration</link>.

Title: Punishment
Text:
When you have a grievance against someone, it is not <link="morality">dishonorable</link> to punish them in proportion to their crime. As a <link="head">ruler</link>, others will come to you asking for justice for crimes against them, and you will be honor-bound to punish their offenders.

Any action that would normally be considered a crime can serve as a punishment. Go to <link="war">war</link> against a ruler who has wronged you and your aggression will be seen as a righteous punishment in the court of public <link="opinion">opinion</link>. There are also some actions you can take specifically to punish your subjects. As the ruler of a <link="colony">colony</link> you can punish inhabitants of your star system through, in order of severity: execution, exile, and nerve-whipping. You can also punish your rulers by levying a fine on them.

You may be tempted to use execution to be rid of a troublesome character, even without justification.

Title: Forming a Vassal Faction
Text:
<link="faction">Factions</link> come into being either through <link="rebellionbetrayal">rebellion</link>, or when the <link="head">ruler</link> of a large faction carves up their territory to make it more <link="vassallimit">manageable</link>.

An independent <link="head">duke</link> or <link="head">archon</link> forms a <link="vassalage">vassal</link> faction by choosing one of their <link="head">barons</link> and granting them ownership over some of the other <link="colony">colonies</link> in their faction (Note: the actions to form a vassal faction and <link="give">transfer a system</link> to it are separate in the UI).

This makes that baron a duke, although they remain a vassal. The master faction of the new vassal faction is immediately considered to have a legitimate <link="claims">claim</link> to being the master of that faction.

Note that vassal dukes cannot form vassal factions, as they cannot themselves have vassals that are dukes. An independent duke forming a vassal faction becomes the archon of a <link="league">league</link>.

Instead of forming a new vassal faction, a duke can resurrect a dead one if they do so while championing a character's claim to lead it. The resurrected faction is immediately granted any colonies to which it has a stronger owning claim than the duke's faction. It is possible for a vassal duke to resurrect a dead faction, but it will become the vassal of their archon.

Title: Rebellion and Betrayal
Text:
Because a <link="vassalage">vassal</link> wields the <link="fleet">military power</link> of their <link="map">territory</link>, a ruler's power is in great part based on their ability to retain the <link="opinion">loyalty</link> of their subjects. Vassals enjoy a great degree of freedom; as long as they do not oppose their master, they may act politically and militarily to their own advantage.

A popular <link="head">baron</link> or vassal <link="head">duke</link> may rebel against their master, hoping to gain enough support to become independent and withstand military retaliation. A less powerful ruler on the edge of their master's territory may choose to betray their allegiance to a neighbour. Both actions are normally <link="morality">dishonorable</link>.

When a baron rebels, a new <link="faction">faction</link> is formed that is immediately at <link="war">war</link> with the parent faction. If the latter was part of a <link="league">league</link>, the rebel faction remains part of it as well. Any other barons that join the rebellion who are <link="claims">legitimate</link> rulers of their colonies grant the rebel faction a claim on their colony. Any faction that has a master claim on the parent faction gains a master claim on the rebel faction.

When a duke rebels, they become independent. If other vassal dukes join the rebellion they form a rebel <link="league">league</link> and become its archon. If the other dukes that join the rebellion are legitimate rulers of their faction, the rebel league is granted a claim on that faction. In either case, the rebel is at war with their former master.

If a league loses its last vassal faction, it is disbanded and its archon becomes a duke.

Title: Surrender
Text:
When a <link="faction">faction</link> or <link="league">league</link> is weak, its <link="head">ruler</link> may not be able to hold on to their independence. They may seek to become a <link="vassalage">vassal</link> of a more powerful ruler, or they may be forced to surrender their <link="domain">domain</link>.

When a ruler surrenders, they become a <link="head">baron</link> within their master's faction, ruling over their <link="colony">home system</link>. All their previous vassals become vassals of their new master. If a <link="head">duke</link> or <link="head">archon</link> surrenders to a vassal duke, that duke becomes an archon and forms a new league independent of their previous league. This is not <link="morality">dishonorable</link>.

You will lose the game if you are no longer a duke.

Title: Deposing a Vassal
Text:
When the relationship between a <link="head">duke</link> or <link="head">archon</link> and one of their <link="vassalage">vassals</link> breaks down, the master may try to replace the vassal with another character through the use of <link="fleet">force</link>. This is normally <link="morality">dishonorable</link>.

A vassal will react to your attempt to depose them in one of three ways;
- They may accept their fate and abdicate the rule of their <link="colony">colony</link> or <link="faction">faction</link> to your chosen replacement.
- They may start a <link="rebellionbetrayal">rebellion</link>, potentially drawing other disaffected vassals to their cause. This is normally dishonorable.
- They may simply refuse to accept the order. If their <link="colony">home system</link> is directly <link="map">nearby</link> to the remainder of your territory you will immediately attack them, replacing them if you win the ensuing <link="combat">combat</link>. Otherwise, they simply become independent and in a state of <link="war">war</link> with you.

Title: Visibility
Text: What is visible to you depends on the knowledge of the character that you are currently playing. Other characters have partial visibility as well. You can see if a character knows another by focusing the first character and contrasting the second. Characters You will always be aware of; - The rulers inside your territory - The dukes and archons whose territory borders yours - The barons whose colonies are on the border your faction - The heirs of any rulers you know - Close members of your family - Members of your house - Nobles that live on your capital or are visiting it You will become aware of other characters organically. There will frequently be events involving someone you do not know. When you switch to a new player character, you will lose visibility of any characters the new player character is not aware of. Houses You are aware of a house if you are aware of its head. Systems You are always aware of any systems in your territory and the territory of nearby factions. Once you learn of a system, you will retain visibility of that system for the rest of the game. Factions and Leagues You are always aware of any nearby factions, and the factions that are nearby to those factions. You learn of a faction if you learn of its ruler. Once you learn of a faction, you will retain visibility of that faction for the rest of the game. You are aware of a league if you are aware of its archon and their faction.

Title: Traits
Text:
Every character in the game has a small set of personality traits that modify their <link="happiness">emotional reaction</link> to events, their base <link="opinion">opinion</link> of other characters, their reputation, their <link="skill">skills</link>, and their behaviour. Focus on a character and hover over their trait icons to see the effect of each trait.

Personality traits come in pairs that are mutually exclusive. A character who has a personality trait will usually like characters with the same trait, and dislike characters with the opposing trait.

The personality traits are;
- Kind or Cruel
- Brave or Cowardly
- Loyal or Fickle
- Greedy or Satisfied
- Friendly or Reserved
- Honorable or Rule-Breaker
- Proud or Humble
- Vengeful or Forgiving
- Charming or Dull
- Tribal or Individualistic
- Intelligent or Stupid

In addition a character can have the Gay trait or the Bisexual trait. These effect whether they can initiate a same sex marriage and the happiness they get from being <link="marriage">married</link>. Note that a marriage between a man and woman will produce children even if one or both characters are Gay.

Children acquire traits gradually as they get older, and they frequently adopt the personality traits of their parents or their <link="guardianship">guardian</link>. They may acquire the Gay trait or the Bisexual trait when they come of age.

Title: Assignments
Text: Members of your house can be assigned to tasks. These tasks, or assignments, provide a variety of benefits. An assignment either completes after a number of turns, or has an ongoing effect each turn it is active. You can stop an assignment at any time. If you stop a completeable assignment before it is finished, half of its <#dcab00> cost is refunded. Many assignments happen outside your home system. The character that is assigned to the task can either carry it out personally (by travelling to the assignment's location) or remotely (by working through agents). Assignments carried out personally are more effective, if you are willing to risk foul play against your house member. Council members cannot travel, and will always carry out their assignments remotely. Each assignment is carried out at an Effectiveness level (1-100). At higher levels, ongoing assignments will have stronger effects, and completeable assignments will finish quicker. Effectiveness is based on: - The level of the assigned character in a specific skill. Each type of assignment relies on one skill. - Whether the character is carrying out the assignment personally or remotely - The happiness of the assigned character - The assigned character's opinion of you You can assign tasks to any adult member of your house except yourself, but the context actions menu on a character will only show the assignments related to their best skill. You can still assign them to other tasks if you trigger the assignment from the context menu of its target. You cannot assign multiple characters to the same assignment.

Title: Love and Affairs
Text:
Characters will sometimes fall in love with other characters. A character in love will be distracted and have a penalty to their skills unless they are married or in an affair with their love interest. Attraction to someone who is not your <link="marriage">spouse</link> is a <link="secret">secret</link>.

You can propose to have an affair with your love interest. Affairs, even between unmarried characters, are <link="morality">dishonorable</link> and are <link="secret">secret</link>. Affairs generate an ongoing positive <link="happiness">happiness</link> emotion on the couple. It is possible for a child to be born from an affair, but it is unlikely.

Title: Map
Text: The map of the galaxy consists of a set of star systems linked together using star lanes. Some star systems contain a colony, while others are empty. Colonies are ruled by a baron. There are 115 colonies, although some may be derelict. Colonies are grouped into factions. Factions are ruled by a duke. Factions may be grouped into leagues. Leagues are ruled by an archon. Two colonies are considered nearby to each other if there is a star lane path between them with no other colony blocking it and that is no more than three "hops" in length. Similarly factions or leagues are considered nearby to each other if there is at least one colony in the first that is nearby to a colony in the other.

Title: Military Conquest
Text:
When you are at <link="war">war</link> with a <link="faction">faction</link> or <link="league">league</link>, you can attack a <link="colony">colony</link> in its territory. This triggers a combat between you and the <link="head">duke</link> that rules that colony's faction.

If you win the combat, you determine the fate of the colony and its <link="head">baron</link>. However, if you are the <link="vassalage">vassal</link> of an <link="head">archon</link> who is at war championing a <link="claims">claim</link> that relates to that colony, they may step in at this point and take these decisions away from you.

Your first decision will be whether to leave its existing baron in place or install a new one. Then, if the war was declared to champion a claim and conquering the colony allows you to <link="championing">press</link> the claim, you will be <link="morality">honor-bound</link> to do so at this point. Lastly, if you are an archon, you choose whether to keep the colony in your faction or to grant it to a nearby vassal faction. Annexing a colony in a faction that has no claim to it is dishonorable, even if the system is conquered in a justified war.

If you conquered the capital system of your enemy, the war will end. Conquering a faction's capital will splinter it into independent colonies. Conquering a league's capital will splinter it into independent factions.

Title: Raids
Text: Each turn, a colony accrues loot, up to a maximum defined by how well repaired the colony is. Loot is the valuable material that can be carried off easily from the colony. A baron may attack a colony in an attempt to plunder its loot. A raid triggers a normal combat to determine whether they succeed. Dukes and archons cannot raid. A duke or archon attacking a system is always attempting to conquer it.

Title: Favours
Text: When a character grants a significant boon to another character without having been obliged, a favour is created. This includes; - Helping a ruler in combat when there is no feudal or kinship obligation - Giving a ruler a colony - Giving a ruler a faction - Granting a vassal independence - Promoting a house member to your council If a character asks for a similar boon from someone who owes them a favour, the latter is honor-bound to reciprocate.

Title: Give Vassal
Text:
A <link="head">duke</link> or <link="head">archon</link> can transfer ownership of a vassal <link="colony">colony</link> in their <link="faction">faction</link> to another duke or archon. An archon can also transfer ownership of a vassal faction in their <link="league">league</link> to another archon or independent duke. The vassal ruler does not have a choice in the matter. 

A vassal duke cannot be granted ownership of a vassal faction. An archon that gives away their last vassal faction becomes a duke.

If done voluntarily and not as part of a trade, this is a <link="favour">favour</link>. Furthermore, the granting ruler weakens their claim to that piece of territory.

Unless a <link="claims">claim</link> is involved, a colony can only be transferred to a faction that it is <link="map">nearby</link> to. Similarly, a faction can only be transferred to a league that it is nearby to. A ruler cannot give away part of their territory if it is nearby to the territory of a ruler they are at <link="war">war</link> with, or if they are at war contesting a claim to it.

Title: Negotiation
Text:
When you make an offer or request to a <link="head">ruler</link>; that ruler may accept, refuse, or reply with a request of their own. In the latter case, you can accept or refuse the suggested trade. Accepting some offers is accepting a <link="favour">favour</link>.

When a ruler makes an offer or request to you, you will be able to counter with any request that you could currently make of them.

When you make the initial request, you can accompany it with a threat. A ruler can only accept or refuse such a request. If they refuse, the threat is automatically carried out. Threats are normally <link="morality">dishonorable</link>.

By hovering over a request or trade, you can find out if a ruler will either definitely accept or definitely refuse. The game will not predict the outcome when the character could reasonably go either way. However the game will show you the precise factors that the character weighed up in arriving to their decision after you make the request.

Demands made when championing a <link="claims">claim</link> are not predicted.

Title: Fleet Composition
Text:
Vessels in a <link="fleet">fleet</link> are classified into one of three types;
- <#043F48FF><sprite name="vessel_bomber" tint=1></color> Bombers
- <#990E0EFF><sprite name="vessel_interceptor" tint=1></color> Interceptors
- <#936100FF><sprite name="vessel_frigate" tint=1></color> Frigates

Each vessel type is strong against one type of vessel, and weak against another.
- <color=#043f48><sprite name="vessel_bomber" tint=1></color> Bombers deal <pv>200%</pv> damage to <color=#936100><sprite name="vessel_frigate" tint=1></color> Frigates and <nv>50%</nv> damage to <color=#990e0e><sprite name="vessel_interceptor" tint=1></color> Interceptors
- <color=#990e0e><sprite name="vessel_interceptor" tint=1></color> Interceptors deal <pv>200%</pv> damage to <color=#043f48><sprite name="vessel_bomber" tint=1></color> Bombers and <nv>50%</nv> damage to <color=#936100><sprite name="vessel_frigate" tint=1></color> Frigates
- <color=#936100><sprite name="vessel_frigate" tint=1></color> Frigates deal <pv>200%</pv> damage to <color=#990e0e><sprite name="vessel_interceptor" tint=1></color> Interceptors and <nv>50%</nv> damage to <color=#043f48><sprite name="vessel_bomber" tint=1></color> Bombers

You can gradually modify the composition of the fleet that is maintained by a specific <link="colony">colony</link> using the <link="technology">Shift Fleet Composition</link> <link="assignments">assignment</link>.

Vessel types also get different bonuses in <link="combat">combat</link> from <link="combattactic">combat tactics</link>.

Title: Marriage Authority
Text:
The <link="marriage">marriage</link> authority of a character is the house <link="head">head</link> who has the right to arrange their marriage or divorce it.

Normally the head of a house is the marriage authority for the members of their house (including themselves), but the following rules override that. In order of priority:
- The ruler of a <link="domain">domain</link> is the marriage authority for all their descendants that live in that domain. If a character descends from two rulers whose domain overlaps, the <link="vassalage">higher ranking</link> ruler is their marriage authority.
- The ruler of a domain is the marriage authority for all their close* genetic relatives that live in that domain. If a character is closely genetically related to two rulers whose domain overlaps, the higher ranking ruler is their marriage authority.

If a character's marriage authority is not the head of their house, they will have a state icon on their character summary indicating this.

Note that while there is only ever one marriage authority that can agree to a marriage for a particular character, there may be two marriage authorities that have the power to divorce the marriage (one for each partner).


*Close genetic relatives are defined as: parents, siblings, children, grandparents, grandchildren, full siblings of your parents, children of full siblings.

Title: Installations
Text:
A <link="colony">colony</link> is made up of <h>installations</h>, i.e. the bases and space stations that are located in a single system. These assets were built before the Collapse by the various states and organizations that were exploring and exploiting the galaxy. Today, they are the only living space left to humanity, and we do not have the capability to build more.

You can see the installations in a colony by hovering over it's star system on the map, or by clicking on it.

Installations are either <h>Functional</h> or <h>in Disrepair</h>. You can repair installations to make use of them using the <h>Repair Installation</h> <link="assignments">assignment</link>. This will provide a benefit that is unique to that installation type.

Installations can suffer collateral damage when there is <link="combat">fighting</link> in the system, and fall back into disrepair. If all the installations in a colony are damaged, the colony is <link="damagedcolony">abandoned</link>.

Normally, installations provide a benefit primarily or solely to the direct ruler of the colony in which they reside. This means that while the installations on your system are always useful to you, the installations in your vassals' colonies might not be.

Some installations are <h>Ranged</h>, indicated by an orange symbol in the bottom left corner of their image. Ranged installations provide one or more benefits to all allied rulers within an area of the map. This makes them valuable to you even when they are outside of your home system.

Title: Combat Tactics
Text: In each round of the resolution phase of combat, both fleet commanders simultaneously choose a combat tactic. A tactic is a collection of tactic effects that stay in play for the remainder of that combat. A tactic effect typically provides a bonus or penalty to combat calculations. A tactic can only be played once per combat, except for the default tactics of Attack and Retreat. Most tactic effects have a type, which is <#D91C25FF>, <#03C2DEFF>, or <#7335ADFF>. Some tactics can remove from play any opponent tactic effects of a specific type. This applies to effects that were played in the current or previous turns. Tactic effects that do not have a type will remain in place once played. Characters learn tactics automatically as their Military skill increases, up to a maximum of 3. In a specific battle you have access to; - Two default tactics: Attack and Retreat - The tactics that are known by the commander leading the fleet - The tactics that are known by the Head of Military of your house Note that if you pick your Head of Military to lead the fleet, each of their tactics will be available twice in that combat.

Title: Arrest
Text:
A character can be arrested by the <link="head">ruler</link> of the <link="colony">colony</link> in which they are currently located. This is normally <link="morality">dishonorable</link>. Arrested characters are held on the colony until the ruler releases them, and their actions are restricted. You can ask a ruler to release a member of your <link="house">house</link> which they have arrested.

Arresting a character halts any troublesome <link="assignments">assignment</link> they could be working on.

You will automatically arrest any members of another house if a <link="war">war</link> starts that makes you an enemy of that house. This is not dishonorable. When you declare war on another ruler, you will automatically recall your house members home from enemy territory before they can be arrested. Any members of your enemy's house that are anywhere in your territory are arrested and transferred to your home system.

Title: Expedition Events
Text:
The remnants of humanity live within the ruins of a civilization that was at the cusp of a golden era of space colonization. We live inside structures which we cannot build, and travel inside machines whose workings are unfathomable. We may not understand it, but technology gives us life and protects us from the harsh universe. And it is a source of power. Within the husks of abandoned colonies, lost spaceships, and other mysterious sightings; lie trinkets that could bring your house glory.

Your <link="house">house</link> strives to discover these relics from <link="collapse">pre-Collapse history</link>, and investigate other mysteries of the galaxy. All in an effort to gain an edge on our rivals.

<h>Expedition Events</h> are story events about these efforts and adventures. They usually, but not always, come with good rewards.

Every turn you gain <h>Expedition Points</h>. You gain more if your house has a higher <link="technology">Technology</link> <link="houseareas">score</link>. Your progress is shown in a bar on the bottom right toolbar. Hover over this to see how many points you have, and how much you are gaining each turn. When you reach a threshold, an Expedition Event triggers.

Title: Guardianship
Text: Note: This feature requires the Bloodlines DLC When a child in your house who is related to you is between the ages of 6 and 16, you can assign them a guardian. The responsibility of the guardian is to safeguard the child and mentor them in a particular skill. The characters that are eligible to be guardians are yourself and the members of your council, and a character may only have one ward at a time. While a child is the ward of a guardian, they will acquire skill points in the best and second best skills of that guardian. Furthermore, the child may also pick up the personality traits of that guardian. You may ask another ruler to be the guardian of a child in your house, or you may be asked to become the guardian of another ruler's child. A ruler whose child you are the guardian of is likely to be significantly more loyal, because they will fear you harming the child while they are in your care. Similarly you should tread carefully around a ruler to whom you have sent one of your relatives as a ward. However rulers will also be pleased when you trust them in this way, so sending children as wards can help you build relationships with other rulers.

Title: Succession
Text: Note: This feature requires the Bloodlines DLC A succession rule identifies the heir who will inherit the rule of a faction or system when its ruler is deceased, and the wider line of succession following that heir. There are four base succession rules: - Oldest Child - Youngest Child - Closest Relative - Oldest Sibling Each base succession rule also has two variants that prefer heirs of one sex over the other. The ruler of a star system or faction can change the succession rule that is law for that domain. This is usually dishonorable, as it is unfair to the current heir, tears up existing tradition, and potentially reduces the value of your political marriages to other houses. A less dishonorable route is to disinherit your current heir without outright changing the succession law - the character who was second in line then becomes the heir. You can also choose to overrule the succession law for your domain and appoint a house member or subject kin member as your heir, however this is the most dishonorable option of all as you are making a mockery of the tradition of bloodline inheritance.
